summary: Extends RFC 1958 with philosophical guidelines for architects and designers of Internet backbone networks. It describes the Simplicity Principle, which holds that complexity is the main thing that prevents efficient scaling, and discusses what that means for design and engineering of large backbones.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3439 is an essay on how to build large Internet networks. Its central claim is that complexity is the main thing that stops big networks from working well, and that adding layers, features and clever optimisations to the middle of the network usually makes things worse rather than better. It is written to extend the principles in RFC 1958.

subtitle: Why the authors of this memo argue that complexity, not function, is what stops large networks scaling

tldr.problem: Large carrier networks behave differently from small ones: small faults cause large outages, features pile up in the core, and the complexity of running them is hard to predict.
tldr.mechanism: The memo names a Simplicity Principle, that complexity is the main thing that prevents efficient scaling and the main driver of both capital and operating cost, and then applies it to layering, convergence, interworking, packet switching and reliability engineering.
tldr.outcome: Several accepted beliefs fall: layering, optimisation, feature richness and universal interworking are all described as harmful, and packet switching is shown to be more complex than circuit switching rather than less. The memo is a philosophy for backbone architects, not a protocol.

today: RFC 3439 is an Informational memo from December 2002 that updates RFC 1958 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It is a philosophy for backbone architects rather than a specification, and its security considerations section notes only that the document does not directly affect the security of any existing Internet protocol, while a system that grows more complex becomes harder to model and analyse and so harder to reason about its security.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
RFC 1958 describes the underlying principles of the Internet architecture. This memo extends that work by outlining philosophical guidelines for architects and designers of Internet backbone networks. The authors warn that many of the areas covered are controversial, but that the unifying principle should not be. Complexity in carrier networks can derive from many sources, and as stated in their reference to Doyle, complexity in most systems is driven by the need for robustness to uncertainty in their environments and component parts far more than by basic functionality. The major thrust of the document is to raise awareness about the complexity of current architectures and to examine the effect that complexity will almost certainly have on the carrier industry's ability to succeed.

The Simplicity Principle, which the authors say was perhaps first articulated by Mike O'Dell, former Chief Architect at UUNET, states that complexity is the primary mechanism which impedes efficient scaling, and as a result is the primary driver of increases in both capital expenditures and operational expenditures. The implication for carrier IP networks is that to be successful, architectures and designs must be driven toward the simplest possible solutions.

The principle is linked to the end-to-end argument, quoted from Saltzer, that end-to-end protocol design should not rely on the maintenance of state inside the network, and that such state should be maintained only in the end points, in such a way that it can only be destroyed when the end point itself breaks. In the hourglass formulation of the Internet architecture, the thin waist is the minimalist IP layer, so the complexity of the Internet belongs at the edges and the IP layer should remain as simple as possible. The authors note that this does not mean the core holds no state, since a huge amount of coarse-grained state such as routing state is maintained there; the important point is that this coarse-grained state is almost orthogonal to the state kept by the end points, and it is this minimisation of interaction that contributes to simplicity. They add that considering the interaction between core and end-point state is crucial when analysing protocols such as Network Address Translation, which reduces the transparency between network and hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo's one rule is simple: complexity is what stops big networks working, so keep the network simple and push the clever parts to the edges. The paper also argues that because complexity is mostly there to survive uncertainty, it tends to create new fragilities as it goes.

sections.title: How Large Systems Amplify Small Changes
sections.content:
The largest networks exhibit, in theory and in practice, architecture, design and engineering non-linearities which smaller networks do not. The authors call this ADE non-linearity, and base it on two principles from non-linear systems theory.

The Amplification Principle states that there are non-linearities which occur at large scale and do not occur at small to medium scale. The corollary is that in many large networks, even small things can and do cause huge events, because small perturbations on the input to a process can destabilise the system's output. A good example is non-linear resonant amplification, where small fluctuations accumulate and, if they are synchronised with other cycles, may produce major changes; the authors point to the destruction of the Tacoma Narrows bridge, the gaps in the asteroid belts and rings of Saturn, and the cycles of the moon and sun. In the Internet domain, more inter-connectivity results in more complex and often slower BGP routing convergence, and a small amount of inter-connectivity causes the output of a routing mesh to be significantly more complex than its input. An important method for reducing amplification is to ensure that local changes have only local effect. ATM provides another example: if you lose one cell, you destroy the entire packet, and without mechanisms such as Early Packet Discard you will keep carrying the already damaged packet. The Boeing 777 example shows the same thing in engineering terms: a fly-by-wire aircraft containing as many as 150,000 subsystems and approximately 1000 CPUs is robust to large disturbances but could be catastrophically disabled by microscopic alterations in a very few large CPUs.

The Coupling Principle states that as things get larger, they often exhibit increased interdependence between components, with the corollary that the more events that occur simultaneously, the more likely it is that two or more will interact, a phenomenon also termed unforeseen feature interaction. Horizontal coupling is exhibited between the same protocol layer, and vertical coupling occurs between layers. Coupling is intimately related to synchronisation, and injecting randomness into these systems is one way to reduce it. The 1991 outage of AT&T's SS7 network is the authors' example of what a tightly coupled complex system can do: one switch crashed because of a hardware glitch, and when it came back up it caused its neighbours to crash, and when they came back up they caused theirs to crash. The root cause turned out to be a misplaced break statement, which the authors call an excellent example of cross-layer coupling.

The voice network supplies a lesson in complexity. In the 1970s and 1980s the voice carriers competed by adding features which drove substantial increases in the complexity of the PSTN, especially in Class 5 switching infrastructure. That complexity was software-based rather than hardware-driven, and therefore had cost curves worse than Moore's Law, so poor margins on voice products today are due to capital and operating costs not dropping as we would expect. The same issue appears when adding a service: the traditional voice network has little intelligence in its edge devices and a very smart core, so a new service means upgrading the whole core, while the Internet has smart edges and a simple core, so adding a service is a matter of distributing an application to the few consenting desktops that want it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things change as a network grows. Small disturbances get amplified, so a single switch rebooting can take down its neighbours. And the parts of the network become more tightly tied together, so more of them can fail each other at once. The telephone network is the example of what happens when features pile up in the core.

sections.title: Layering, Convergence and the Cell Tax
sections.content:
A layer in the networking sense implements one or more of error control, flow control, fragmentation, multiplexing, connection setup and addressing or naming. Layering has conceptual advantages, but in data networking it means that the functions of each layer are carried out completely before the data is passed to the next layer, so each layer must be optimised separately, and that ordering conflicts with efficient implementation. One could accuse the layered model of TCP/IP and ISO OSI of causing this conflict: the operations of multiplexing and segmentation both hide information that lower layers may need to optimise their performance, layer N may duplicate lower level functionality such as hop-by-hop rather than end-to-end error recovery, and different layers may need the same information. As a result of inter-layer dependencies, increased layering quickly violates the Simplicity Principle, and the first order conclusion is that horizontal separation may be more cost-effective and reliable in the long term.

Three corollaries follow. Optimisation is considered harmful, because it introduces complexity and tighter coupling, and because of the Law of Diminishing Returns, squeezing out efficiency past a certain point only adds complexity and leads to less reliable systems. Feature richness is considered harmful, because the danger is increased system complexity. And the evolution of transport infrastructure for IP shows what removing layers buys: IP over ATM over SONET, then IP over SONET over WDM, then IP over WDM, with decreasing complexity, capital cost and operating cost, because layers are removed.

Convergence is related, since convergence is achieved via a convergence layer, and the end state of the argument is the concept of Everything Over Some Layer. Conduit, DWDM, fibre, ATM, MPLS and even IP have all been proposed as convergence layers, and since layering typically drives operating cost up, the authors expect convergence to as well. The most germane example of convergence layer failure is IP over ATM, and the immediate consequence of ATM layering is the so-called cell tax. Recent data shows that about 95% of WAN bytes and 85% of packets are TCP, and much of this traffic is composed of 40 and 44 byte packets. The 8-byte SNAP header is what causes most of the problems, forcing most small packets to consume two cells with the second cell mostly empty padding, which costs about another 16% of the ideal throughput. For a DS3 line the result is a line rate of 44.736 Mbps, less 4.032 for PLCP overhead, less 3.840 for per cell headers and less 5.900 for the SNAP header and padding, leaving 30.960 Mbps, so the total overhead is about 31%.

Layering also produces unanticipated second order effects. The classic study of TCP good-put over ATM found that large UBR buffers, larger than one TCP window, are required to achieve reasonable performance, and that packet discard mechanisms improve effective bandwidth usage. The same kind of problem appears with IP transport's implicit assumptions of lower layers: TCP assumes packet losses mean congestion, when sometimes they come from corruption on a wireless link; TCP assumes significantly reordered packets mean congestion, which is not always the case; TCP assumes a missing acknowledgement within a period based on the measured round-trip time means packet loss; and TCP congestion control assumes all packets in a flow are treated the same by the network. Finally, the base assumption that Everything over IP will produce capital and operating cost efficiencies requires critical examination, because a more efficient convergence layer might be much lower in the stack, and building an IP network with SONET-like restoration times could cost more than building the SONET network in the first place.
sections.plainLanguage: Stacking layers on top of each other makes each one optimise separately and hides information the layer below needs. IP over ATM is the worked example: the 8-byte header on each ATM cell makes small packets need two cells, and on a DS3 line the overhead comes to about 31%.

sections.title: Avoid the Universal Interworking Function
sections.content:
While there have been many implementations of Universal Interworking Function, IWF approaches have been problematic at large scale. The concern is codified in the Principle of Minimum Intervention: to minimise the scope of information, and to improve the efficiency of data flow through the encapsulation layer, the payload should, where possible, be transported as received without modification.

The corollary is to avoid control plane interworking. Integrated solutions perform poorly at both ends of the performance and cost spectrum: the protocols with the least switching demand may have to bear the cost of the most expensive, while the protocols with the most stringent requirements often have to make concessions to those with different requirements. Interworking functions should therefore be restricted to data plane interworking and encapsulations, and these functions should be carried out at the edge of the network. The trade-off is often described as the Integrated versus Ships In the Night trade-off, and in general there are few cases in which such integrated solutions have proven efficient. Multi-protocol BGP is a subtly different and notable exception, because the control plane there is independent of the format of the control data, so no control plane data conversion is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not build a box that translates everything into everything. Keep translation to the data path, and put it at the edge of the network, so the middle stays simple.

sections.title: Packet Switching Is Not Simpler Than Circuit Switching
sections.content:
Conventional wisdom holds that packet switching is inherently more efficient than circuit switching, because of statistical multiplexing and hop-by-hop forwarding decisions, and it is widely assumed that IP is simpler than circuit switching and should be more economical to deploy and manage. The authors examine these assumptions and find a different picture.

On efficiency, Odlyzko and Coffman report average utilisation of links in IP networks in the range between 3% and 20%, with corporate intranets at the 3% level and commercial Internet backbones at 15 to 20%, against about 33% for long haul voice lines. The reasons they cite for the low figures are that Internet traffic is extremely asymmetric and bursty while links are symmetric and of fixed capacity, that it is difficult to predict traffic growth on a link so operators add bandwidth aggressively, and that falling prices for coarser bandwidth granularity make it appear more economical to add capacity in large increments.

On simplicity, today's Internet backbone routers are extremely complex and that complexity scales with line rate. Since a direct comparison has resisted analysis, the authors use observable artifacts. Software: the typical software image for an Internet router requires between eight and ten million instructions including firmware, while a typical transport switch requires on average about three million; the AT&T 5ESS class 5 switch, with a huge number of calling features, needs only about twice the lines of code of an Internet core router. Operations: a router's line card must process the packet header, do longest prefix match, generate ICMP error messages, process IP header options and buffer packets so that TCP congestion control works, which typically requires a buffer holding around 250 ms of packet data, and this does not include route and packet filtering or any quality of service or VPN filtering, while a transport switch need only map ingress time-slots to egress time-slots and interfaces. Hardware: an OC192 POS router line card contains at least 30 million gates in ASICs, at least one CPU, 300 Mbytes of packet buffers, 2 Mbytes of forwarding table and 10 Mbytes of other state memory, against 7.5 million logic gates, no CPU, no packet buffer, no forwarding table and on-chip state memory for a comparable transport switch line card. Power and density follow: the highest capacity transport switches have about four times the capacity of an IP router and sell for about one third as much per Gigabit per second.

The authors identify the fundamental driver as the hop-by-hop independence inherent in the IP architecture, in contrast to the end-to-end architectures such as ATM or Frame Relay, and they cite a complexity and robustness spiral in which increases in complexity create further and more serious sensitivities, which then require additional robustness. The lesson they draw is that the Simplicity Principle applies to circuit switching too, but is crucial in controlling the complexity of packet networks. The major operating cost challenge for IP is that debugging a large-scale IP network still requires a large degree of expertise, because you may have to visit a large set of your routers only to discover that the problem is external to your own network.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual claim is that packets are simpler than circuits. Measuring the actual machines says otherwise: a backbone router runs three times as much software as a transport switch and its line card has four times as many logic gates. The extra work comes from each router deciding what to do with each packet on its own.

sections.title: Over-Provisioning, Five Nines and the Proportionality Law
sections.content:
The memo treats two widely held beliefs as myths. The first is over-provisioning. The desire of network engineers to keep utilisation below 50% has been called over-provisioning, but the authors say the term is a misnomer: in modern Internet backbones the unused capacity is actually protection capacity, which can be viewed as one-to-one protection at the IP layer, so an IP network provisioned to run at 50% utilisation is no more over-provisioned than a typical SONET network. The advantages that accrue include close to speed of light delay and close to zero packet loss. There are system-theoretic reasons for this too: packet-switched networks with in-band control loops can become unstable when congested, congestion in one part of the network spreads to other parts, and when routing protocol packets are lost the result can be traffic loops, black holes and lost connectivity.

The second myth is five nines. Since 80% of unscheduled outages are caused by people or process errors, there is only a 20% window in which to optimise, so increasing component reliability means adding complexity, which is the root cause of 80% of the unplanned outages. This narrows the window further, which the authors characterise as a complexity and robustness spiral. The conclusion is that while a system like the Internet can reach five-nines-like reliability, it is undesirable, and likely impossible, to try to make any individual component, especially the most complex ones, reach that standard.

The third idea offered is the Architectural Component Proportionality Law, which states that the complexity of an architecture is proportional to its number of components, and that the probability of achieving a stable implementation of an architecture is inversely proportional to its number of components. Components include discrete elements such as hardware, space and power requirements, as well as software, firmware and the protocols they implement. The corollary is to minimise the number of components in a service delivery path, which can be a protocol path, a software path or a physical path, because the path between a customer and the desired service is particularly sensitive to the number and complexity of elements in it. The authors give examples of architectures that never found a market because of this effect, such as TINA-based CRM systems and CORBA and TINA based service architectures, which could only be deployed as limited scale deployments or with massive investment.

The conclusions restate the Simplicity Principle as the one rule that must be controlled if a complex object is to scale efficiently, and place it in a long line of thought: Occam's Razor, the KISS principle, the Principle of Least Astonishment, and the observation that a trade-off can be made between simplicity of interactions and looseness of coupling. Two of the memo's conclusions are worth singling out. It warns that highly converged approaches are likely to be less efficient than less converged solutions, so the optimal convergence layer may be much lower in the protocol stack than conventionally believed. And it reports that the study finds packet switching to be more complex than circuit switching, a conclusion borne out by the fact that normalized operating cost for data networks is typically significantly greater than for voice networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Running a network at half speed is not waste; the spare capacity is what keeps it working when something fails. And chasing perfect reliability by adding complexity backfires, since most outages come from people and process, not from hardware failing.
